facts.text: Lower Santan Village sits atop a key Hohokam site where artisans crafted specialized pottery along the Middle Gila River during the Classic Period (AD 1150–1450).
The village’s prehistoric legacy links ancient Hohokam inhabitants to today’s Akimel O'odham descendants, forming a foundational element of the Gila River Indian Community.
Lower Santan Village is home to Akimel O'odham (Pima) and Pee‑Posh (Maricopa) tribes, reflecting centuries of cultural heritage along the fertile Sonoran Desert river valley.
Archaeologists uncovered three large circular rock and adobe granary pedestals at Lower Santan, evidence of organized surplus storage in a hinterland near the Hohokam core.
Hohokam farmers at Lower Santan relied on sophisticated irrigation canals from the Gila River, growing maize, beans, squash, and cotton in the desert lowlands.
In 1928, the Coolidge Dam diverted most Gila River water for non‑Indigenous irrigation, sharply reducing downstream flows and crippling traditional farming on the reservation.
